exhibits.title: STARS
exhibits.summary: Fly through the real galaxy — 123,000 stars at their true 3D positions, with instruments no planetarium ships.

sections.inspiration: Everyone builds maps; nobody builds instruments. STARS starts from that thesis: a navigable atlas of the real solar neighbourhood that lets you measure it, not only look at it.
sections.designChallenges: Rendering more than a hundred thousand real stars smoothly in a browser, and keeping the data honest: real data is rendered as real, and anything procedural is labelled.
sections.architecturalDecisions: A Python pipeline packs the AT-HYG catalogue into a compact binary star buffer. A Vite, React and Three.js viewer flies through it with SketchUp-style orbit, pan and zoom, in a galactic frame with the Sun at the origin and one unit per light-year.
sections.implementation: Measurement tethers give the true 3D separation of any two stars; closure rates come from real velocity vectors; relativistic mission briefs give ship time, Earth time and peak γ at constant 1 g; intercept navigation aims where a star will be; deep-time scrubbing runs ±100,000 years. It ships as a static site built by GitHub Actions.
sections.outcomes: Live in the browser, showing 123,018 catalogue stars and 145,128 far-field stars.

exhibits.title: Baduk
exhibits.summary: Learn Go by playing it — four bots with distinct personalities, and a coach that explains every move.

sections.inspiration: A superhuman opponent teaches a beginner almost nothing. Baduk is a place where someone who has never played can sit down, understand what is happening, and enjoy it.
sections.designChallenges: Making bot strength honest. Levels are measured in bot-versus-bot arenas rather than guessed, and nothing claims a calibrated human rank.
sections.architecturalDecisions: The bots and the coach reason from the same evaluator, so the advice a learner reads is the reasoning the opponent actually used. Facts about the position are kept apart from opinions about what to play. It is a static build with no backend; bots run in a Web Worker.
sections.implementation: A rules engine with ko and superko, area and territory scoring, handicap and SGF; four opponents from random play to Monte Carlo tree search; graduated hints; a 15-concept curriculum and post-game review; 170 tests.
sections.outcomes: Measured on 9×9: Sprout beats Pebble 9–0, Kaze beats Sprout 9–3, and Tenuki beats Kaze 5–3 at 600 ms of thinking time.
sections.lessonsLearned: Learners bond with characters more readily than with a difficulty slider, so each opponent has a name, a face and an honest blind spot.
